E1a: at regina gravi iamdudum saucia cura: the book opens with the queen already wounded; iamdudum shows the torment has gone on all night, and gravi … cura makes her love a heavy anxiety
vulnus alit venis: paradox of feeding a wound instead of tending it, so love is a sickness she keeps alive in her own blood
caeco carpitur igni: fire imagery with harsh alliteration of c; the hidden fire eats her away from inside like a fever
multa viri virtus animo multusque recursat gentis honos: repetition of multus and the v alliteration of viri virtus show his qualities returning to torment her mind again and again
haerent infixi pectore vultus verbaque: infixi recalls an arrow driven in, and the enjambment of verbaque makes his words cling on into the next line as they cling in her heart
nec placidam membris dat cura quietem: cura returns from line 1 to enclose the sentence, and the denial of rest shows love as a physical illness that robs her body of sleep
postera Phoebea lustrabat lampade terras: the calm, bright dawn contrasts with the sleepless darkness of Dido's mind, so her torment stands out
cum sic unanimam adloquitur male sana sororem: male sana, literally ‘badly sane’, presents her as sick in mind before she speaks
quae me suspensam insomnia terrent: exclamation; her sleepless nights terrify her and leave her in suspense, the symptoms of a disturbed and suffering mind
E1b: cum sic unanimam adloquitur male sana sororem: male sana warns that Dido's judgement is already unsound as she begins to praise Aeneas
quae me suspensam insomnia terrent: the opening exclamation shows her in a state of breathless excitement, kept awake by him
quis novus hic nostris successit sedibus hospes: rhetorical question; novus and the emphatic hic show her wonder at this stranger who has entered her home
quem sese ore ferens, quam forti pectore et armis: exclamations with anaphora (quem … quam) and a rising tricolon of his looks, courage and arms show how dazzled she is
credo equidem, nec vana fides, genus esse deorum: she insists, with the parenthesis nec vana fides, that he must be descended from gods; her admiration becomes almost worship
degeneres animos timor arguit: a short maxim used to prove his noble birth; she argues like a general to justify her admiration
heu, quibus ille iactatus fatis: the exclamation heu shows pity mixed with admiration for the sufferings he has endured
quae bella exhausta canebat: canebat makes his story sound like an epic song; she is enchanted by him as storyteller as well as warrior
E1c: at regina gravi iamdudum saucia cura: at plunges us into a new scene, and iamdudum opens in the middle of her suffering, a dramatic start
vulnus alit venis et caeco carpitur igni: two vivid images of love, a wound and a hidden fire, introduced together; the alliteration of c makes the fire bite
haerent infixi pectore vultus verbaque: infixi pictures his face and words driven into her heart, and the enjambment of verbaque makes them cling on
nec placidam membris dat cura quietem: cura encloses the opening sentence and the line ends on the rest she cannot have, so we see a sleepless queen
postera Phoebea lustrabat lampade terras umentemque Aurora polo dimoverat umbram: grand epic description of dawn, its light set against the darkness of her night
cum sic unanimam adloquitur male sana sororem: the shift into direct speech brings us close to her disturbed mind, flagged by male sana
quae me suspensam insomnia terrent: Dido's first words are an exclamation of fear and sleeplessness, which makes her voice urgent and immediate
quem sese ore ferens, quam forti pectore et armis: breathless exclamations and a rising tricolon of praise let us hear how dazzled she is
heu, quibus ille iactatus fatis! quae bella exhausta canebat: two further exclamations end the passage on a high pitch of emotion and pity
E2a: si mihi non animo fixum immotumque sederet: the near-synonyms fixum immotumque stress how firm she claims her resolve is, so its collapse shows the strength of the conflict
ne cui me vinclo vellem sociare iugali: marriage pictured as a chain or yoke, something she fears yet is drawn towards
primus amor deceptam morte fefellit: deceptam … fefellit doubles the idea of betrayal; loyalty to her first love pulls against the new
si non pertaesum thalami taedaeque fuisset: two ‘if not’ clauses hold back the main verb, so the conflict is built into the sentence; the alliteration of t stresses her weariness of marriage
huic uni forsan potui succumbere culpae: she admits in potui that she could have given in, while forsan and huic uni try to make it small; calling love a culpa shows her guilt
miseri post fata Sychaei coniugis: miseri shows her continuing pity and love for Sychaeus, which makes the new feelings painful to admit
solus hic inflexit sensus animumque labantem impulit: her heart is a wall already slipping, and the run-over to impulit enacts the push Aeneas has given it
agnosco veteris vestigia flammae: fire imagery; the ‘old flame’ she once felt for Sychaeus is the very feeling that now draws her to Aeneas, so both loves meet in one line
E2b: Anna, fatebor enim: the confession comes first, so the oath that follows is a struggle against what she has just admitted, which adds to its force
sparsos fraterna caede penates: the vivid picture of blood on the household gods recalls the crime that took Sychaeus, giving the oath its painful background

sed mihi vel tellus optem prius ima dehiscat vel pater omnipotens adigat me fulmine ad umbras: two terrible alternatives, from below and from above, linked by vel … vel, show how solemnly she means it
pater omnipotens adigat me fulmine: she calls on Jupiter's thunderbolt, the punishment for oath-breakers, so the oath is sworn before the highest god
ad umbras, pallentes umbras Erebi noctemque profundam: umbras is repeated and expanded into a picture of the dark underworld, making the curse on herself chillingly vivid
ante, pudor, quam te violo aut tua iura resolvo: apostrophe to her own sense of honour as if to a goddess; breaking the oath becomes a kind of sacrilege
ille meos, primus qui me sibi iunxit, amores abstulit: the emphatic ille and the enjambment of abstulit stress that her love belongs to Sychaeus alone
ille habeat secum servetque sepulcro: repeated ille and the alliteration of s close the oath with finality: her love is to stay with him in the grave
sic effata sinum lacrimis implevit obortis: the oath ends in floods of tears, showing how much it costs her to swear it
E2c: si mihi non animo fixum immotumque sederet: the pairing fixum immotumque presents her loyalty as unshakeable, setting up the struggle that follows
primus amor deceptam morte fefellit: her first love is personified as having cheated her by dying; loyalty to it is mixed with hurt
huic uni forsan potui succumbere culpae: after two conditional clauses she admits in potui that she could give way; culpa shows that she already feels the new love as a betrayal
solus hic inflexit sensus animumque labantem impulit: solus hic stresses that only Aeneas has moved her, and the enjambment of impulit shows her wavering heart pushed over
agnosco veteris vestigia flammae: fire imagery joins the two loves: what she feels for Aeneas is the old flame she once felt for Sychaeus
sed mihi vel tellus optem prius ima dehiscat: the strong adversative sed swings her back to loyalty, so the speech enacts the struggle
ante, pudor, quam te violo aut tua iura resolvo: apostrophe to pudor; loyalty to Sychaeus becomes a sacred duty she would rather die than break
ille meos, primus qui me sibi iunxit, amores abstulit; ille habeat secum servetque sepulcro: anaphora of ille points firmly to Sychaeus as she tries to hand her love back to him in the grave
sic effata sinum lacrimis implevit obortis: her speech ends in tears, which suggests that the struggle is far from won
E3a: o luce magis dilecta sorori: Anna opens with hyperbolic affection, loving Dido more than life, which disarms her before the argument begins

solane perpetua maerens carpere iuventa: a rhetorical question, so Dido seems to persuade herself; carpere echoes the wasting of line 2 and perpetua … iuventa stresses how much of her youth would be lost
nec dulces natos Veneris nec praemia noris: nec … nec pairs children and love, the two things a widow gives up, an appeal to her heart
id cinerem aut manes credis curare sepultos: a blunt, dismissive question that reduces Sychaeus to dust and shades, undercutting Dido's oath
esto: aegram nulli quondam flexere mariti: the concession esto grants Dido's past refusals only to turn them against her
non Libyae, non ante Tyro; despectus Iarbas: anaphora of non sweeps quickly through her rejections so Anna can reach her key point
placitone etiam pugnabis amori: the decisive question; placito stresses that this love is welcome, and pugnabis makes resistance sound like a pointless war against herself

hinc Gaetulae urbes, genus insuperabile bello, et Numidae infreni cingunt: anaphora of hinc and the frightening descriptions of warlike neighbours make Carthage seem surrounded and in need of a protector
quid bella Tyro surgentia dicam germanique minas: praeteritio; by saying she will not mention the threat from Tyre and Dido's brother, Anna ends on the most personal danger of all
E3b: o luce magis dilecta sorori: Anna begins with hyperbolic affection, an emotional appeal that comes before any argument
solane perpetua maerens carpere iuventa: she pictures Dido alone, grieving and wasting away; sola placed first stresses her loneliness
perpetua … iuventa: Anna stresses that Dido is still young, so a lifetime of mourning seems a waste
nec dulces natos Veneris nec praemia noris: the pairing of sweet children and the rewards of love appeals to what Dido longs for, made sweeter by dulces
id cinerem aut manes credis curare sepultos: a scornful rhetorical question that reduces the dead Sychaeus to ashes, freeing Dido from guilt
esto: aegram nulli quondam flexere mariti: aegram sympathises with her past grief before turning it into a reason to change
despectus Iarbas ductoresque alii: Anna flatters Dido by recalling the powerful suitors she has scorned, so Aeneas becomes the one man worthy of her
placitone etiam pugnabis amori: the climax of the emotional appeal; Anna names Dido's love as welcome and asks why she should fight it
nec venit in mentem quorum consederis arvis: a further question that asks Dido to look at her situation, gently shifting from feeling to fear
E3c: nec venit in mentem quorum consederis arvis: a rhetorical question that makes Dido face the dangers of her position for herself
hinc Gaetulae urbes, genus insuperabile bello: anaphora of hinc begins a list of enemies; insuperabile bello exaggerates their threat to make protection seem essential
et Numidae infreni cingunt et inhospita Syrtis: polysyndeton and the image of riders ‘without bridles’ make the neighbours wild and lawless, and cingunt shows Carthage surrounded
hinc deserta siti regio lateque furentes Barcaei: even the land is hostile, and late furentes makes the Barcaeans rage far and wide; enjambment carries the threat over the line
quid bella Tyro surgentia dicam germanique minas: praeteritio raises the danger from Tyre and Dido's own brother while claiming to pass over it
dis equidem auspicibus reor et Iunone secunda: the language of official auspices presents the Trojans' arrival as approved by the gods and by Juno, Carthage's own goddess
hunc cursum Iliacas vento tenuisse carinas: the epic adjective Iliacas and the idea that the wind steered them make the alliance seem fated
quam tu urbem, soror, hanc cernes, quae surgere regna coniugio tali: exclamations of a city and kingdom rising; coniugio tali, placed at the start of the line, calls the match a marriage
Teucrum comitantibus armis Punica se quantis attollet gloria rebus: Trojan arms set beside Carthaginian glory turn a love affair into a policy for defence and greatness
E4a: dis equidem auspicibus reor et Iunone secunda: Anna claims the gods and Juno as supporters; the language of auspices gives her vision divine approval
hunc cursum Iliacas vento tenuisse carinas: the epic phrasing and the wind that brought the ships make the future seem planned by fate
quam tu urbem, soror, hanc cernes, quae surgere regna: exclamatory clauses with quam … quae make Dido see the future as if before her eyes; the direct address soror makes it personal
coniugio tali: placed at the start of the line, the word ‘marriage’ is presented as natural, the step on which the whole vision depends
Teucrum comitantibus armis Punica se quantis attollet gloria rebus: Trojan arms and Punic glory are set side by side, and attollet pictures that glory rising like a great building
tu modo posce deos veniam, sacrisque litatis: tu modo makes the path to this future sound easy: only prayer and sacrifice are needed
indulge hospitio causasque innecte morandi: love is dressed up as the duty of a host, and innecte suggests weaving a web of reasons to keep Aeneas
dum pelago desaevit hiems et aquosus Orion, quassataeque rates, dum non tractabile caelum: a tricolon of practical reasons, with repeated dum, makes delay seem sensible
his dictis impenso animum flammavit amore: fire imagery shows the vision working at once, setting Dido's heart ablaze
E4b: quam tu urbem, soror, hanc cernes, quae surgere regna coniugio tali: Anna's excited exclamations paint a future Dido can almost see, and call the match a marriage
Punica se quantis attollet gloria rebus: the promise of Carthaginian glory appeals to Dido the founder and queen
tu modo posce deos veniam: tu modo shrinks the obstacle: all Dido has to do is ask the gods' pardon
indulge hospitio causasque innecte morandi: two short commands; indulge hospitio makes love sound respectable, and innecte pictures a web of excuses to hold Aeneas
dum pelago desaevit hiems et aquosus Orion: heavy d alliteration conveys winter storms that give Dido a ready excuse
quassataeque rates, dum non tractabile caelum: practical details of damaged ships and an unmanageable sky remove her last objections
his dictis impenso animum flammavit amore: the fire imagery and impenso show Anna's words inflaming Dido at once
spemque dedit dubiae menti solvitque pudorem: a tricolon of effects; hope is given, doubt overcome and pudor ‘loosened’, the very honour she swore to keep in line 27
E4c: dis equidem auspicibus reor et Iunone secunda: Anna begins by claiming divine support, choosing Juno, the goddess Dido honours most
hunc cursum Iliacas vento tenuisse carinas: she presents chance as fate, so Aeneas' arrival seems to demand a response
quam tu urbem, soror, hanc cernes, quae surgere regna: vivid exclamations and the affectionate soror appeal to Dido's imagination and to their bond
coniugio tali: Anna slips in the word ‘marriage’ at the start of the line as if it were already agreed
Teucrum comitantibus armis Punica se quantis attollet gloria rebus: she switches to politics, offering Trojan military support and Carthaginian glory, so love seems also to serve the state
tu modo posce deos veniam, sacrisque litatis: a series of easy instructions; tu modo makes the plan simple and respectable
indulge hospitio causasque innecte morandi: skilful euphemism presents love as hospitality, and innecte suggests a cunning plan to delay Aeneas
dum pelago desaevit hiems et aquosus Orion, quassataeque rates, dum non tractabile caelum: a closing tricolon of practical reasons, with anaphora of dum, gives Dido a ready excuse
E5a: principio delubra adeunt pacemque per aras exquirunt: the sisters begin correctly with the gods, but pacem suggests the inner peace Dido cannot find there
mactant lectas de more bidentes: de more stresses that every rite is done properly, which makes its failure all the more striking
legiferae Cereri Phoeboque patrique Lyaeo, Iunoni ante omnes: polysyndeton shows her trying god after god, and the list climaxes on Juno, goddess of marriage
cui vincla iugalia curae: the same bonds of marriage she swore never to enter (line 16) are now what she prays for, so the rites serve her passion
pecudumque reclusis pectoribus inhians spirantia consulit exta: inhians shows her staring hungrily into the opened victims; their opened breasts mirror her own wounded heart
heu, vatum ignarae mentes: the narrator breaks in with heu and an exclamation: even those who read the signs cannot see that Dido is beyond help
quid vota furentem, quid delubra iuvant: two rhetorical questions with anaphora of quid declare the prayers and shrines useless; furentem names her madness
est molles flamma medullas interea: est (‘eats’) and the fire imagery show love consuming her to the marrow while she worships; interea sets the fire against the rites
tacitum vivit sub pectore vulnus: the wound of line 2 returns, silent and alive, with soft v alliteration; no sacrifice can heal it
E5b: ipsa tenens dextra pateram pulcherrima Dido: Dido at her most beautiful, doing the rites herself, which makes her coming suffering more pitiable
pecudumque reclusis pectoribus inhians spirantia consulit exta: the still-breathing victims she stares into foreshadow her own death and link her with the sacrificed
heu, vatum ignarae mentes! quid vota furentem, quid delubra iuvant: the narrator's exclamation and questions show that nothing can save her: she is helpless before her love
est molles flamma medullas interea et tacitum vivit sub pectore vulnus: fire and wound imagery show love attacking her from inside, an enemy she cannot fight
uritur infelix Dido: uritur placed first makes her burning define her, and infelix, her recurring epithet, marks her as doomed
totaque vagatur urbe furens: enjambment spreads her aimless wandering across the line as it spreads through the city; furens shows that she is no longer in control
qualis coniecta cerva sagitta: simile of the wounded deer, a helpless hunted animal; the word order frames cerva with the arrow, pinning her as the arrow does
pastor agens telis liquitque volatile ferrum nescius: the unknowing shepherd stands for Aeneas; nescius, held back to the next line, stresses that she suffers from a wound he did not mean to give
illa fuga silvas saltusque peragrat Dictaeos: the s alliteration conveys her frantic, breathless flight, which cannot rid her of the arrow
haeret lateri letalis harundo: the simile ends on the arrow still fixed in her, and letalis looks ahead to her death; the l sounds slow the line to a close
E5c: principio delubra adeunt pacemque per aras exquirunt: the sisters move from shrine to shrine and altar to altar, a busy, crowded opening
mactant lectas de more bidentes: precise ritual detail of chosen victims slaughtered in the proper way brings the scene before our eyes
legiferae Cereri Phoeboque patrique Lyaeo, Iunoni ante omnes: a list of gods joined by polysyndeton, building to Juno, gives the scene a sense of mounting effort

ipsa tenens dextra pateram pulcherrima Dido candentis vaccae media inter cornua fundit: a precise picture of Dido pouring the libation between the white heifer's horns; ipsa and pulcherrima focus our eyes on her
aut ante ora deum pingues spatiatur ad aras: spatiatur, ‘walks to and fro’, shows her restless movement before the statues of the gods
instauratque diem donis: she renews the day with gifts, sacrificing again and again, which adds to the sense of a long, frantic ritual
pecudumque reclusis pectoribus inhians spirantia consulit exta: gruesome detail of the opened breasts and still-breathing entrails, with inhians showing her open-mouthed stare
heu, vatum ignarae mentes! quid vota furentem, quid delubra iuvant: the narrator's sudden exclamation and questions break the scene, turning description into pathos
est molles flamma medullas interea et tacitum vivit sub pectore vulnus: the passage ends on vivid fire and wound imagery, the hidden reality beneath the public rites
